speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister who will

Oral Questions
know that today the Conference Board has declared that confidence in Canada is at an all-time low. Does the minister recognize that the problem of youth unemployment is serious, and does he agree with what the Minister of Employment and Immigration said yesterday, that we could lose a whole generation of young workers who become frustrated at not being able to find jobs? Will the minister have something to say today which will give young people, who are now being laid off in enormous numbers, some hope that they can play a part in Canada?

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what 1 find to be most encouraging and what I hear about public opinion through the press media and other means is that the people of Canada are now joining in the objective indicated by the Minister of Finance in his budget. I find that wonderful.

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Massive unemployment!

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: I also take satisfaction in the fact that today, for example, the bank rate has come down to 15.6 per cent-

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: -the exchange rate is keeping at 79.35 cents in relation to the U.S. dollar, and the index of industrial production rose by one per cent in May. These are a number of indicators, not of a very rapid change, but of a move, and the same indication comes from the United States. My conclusion, and the Leader of the Opposition will find it professorial, but I will make it nevertheless, is that there are clear indications that if we all hold hands, as one of the hon. members just said, the near future will be much better than appeared in the recent past.

Madam Speaker, we are all wringing our hands and hoping something will happen. The minister will know that, while we are happy to see a drop in the bank rate, it is still one full per cent higher than it was in January when we saw the worst economic performance in one quarter in this country's history. It is all very well for the bank rate to drop a measly 57 basis points, but it is still high. The minister knows that there are young people being laid off and that they are the first to go in any lay-off program. Does the minister appreciate the fact that unemployment of those between the ages of 20 and 24 has risen 60 per cent in a full year? What program does the government have to ensure that it will not be the young people who will pay all the penalty of being first laid off in those parts of government service under federal jurisdiction?
July 22, 1982

speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the issue raised by the hon. member is, of course, of particular concern to the Department of Employment and Immigration. We have the new training legislation passed by Parliament and given royal assent in June, which will be aimed at helping the young across Canada, and we shall therefore be able to provide training for jobs in the high technology sector in this country. Both the department and the government are concerned about youth employment-that was the whole point of our meeting yesterday in Toronto-and we are going to continue our efforts to meet the needs of Canada's young people and provide jobs for them.

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON ACID RAIN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, all members of this House just supported a motion under Standing Order 43 commending very heartily the United States Senate environment committee for its decision earlier today to slash acid rain-causing emissions in that country over the next 12 years. My question to the Minister of the Environment is this. The minister said some weeks ago that Canada might have to withdraw from its negotiations with the United States toward achieving a binding bilateral accord on acid rain because of American foot-dragging on the issue. Will the minister tell the House whether the major breakthrough on acid rain in the U.S. Senate today-it is a major breakthrough-has given the minister and the Canadian government cause to reconsider their threat to withdraw from their negotiations with the Americans on acid rain?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON ACID RAIN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the question, partly because it gives me the opportunity to agree with him that the decision by the United States Senate earlier today is a major breakthrough. I would like to say that there are members on all sides of this House who, through their work with their Congressional counterparts in the United States, have helped to make that favourable event take place today.

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON ACID RAIN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON ACID RAIN
speechtext:
The House earlier today recognized the efforts of Senator Stafford in the United States in that regard. It is important also to recognize the efforts of Senator Mitchell of Maine, and the leading democratic spokesman, Senator Jennings Randolph, and particularly the support which the Senate Leader, Howard Baker of the United States, gave to these efforts. Those decisions by these extremely able, influential and leading American Senators have been very helpful to us.
As the hon. member suggests, this extremely favourable sign should encourage us to continue our work in the United States with the administration, and equally with Congress. In his question the hon. member used the word "threat". I do not think that is a word I have ever used. It was simply a fact of life that, given the delays in the negotiations, it was necessary for us to reassess what position we should take. It is my hope that the scientific group which has been working on this problem will resume its activities in the month of August. When we see the results of those working task forces, we will be able to begin negotiations again early in the autumn. However, it will depend to some extent on whether the task force reports indicate that progress is being made.

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON ACID RAIN

Madam Speaker, every member on this side of the House welcomes that positive reassurance from the minister.

Madam Speaker, I will direct my supplementary to the same minister. Earlier this week Ontario Hydro announced that it is going to shelve plans to instal acid rain controls on its plants in Ontario. Now that we have had a genuine act of good faith by the Americans on the acid rain question, will the minister consider using his good offices to try to convince Ontario Hydro to reverse its decision, as an act of good faith on the part of all Canadians on this important, vital and urgent problem?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Yes, Madam Speaker. I will do everything I can to try to bring to the attention of Ontario Hydro the importance of moving as quickly as possible to introduce and maintain anti-pollution devices which are as effective as possible. I think the important thing to note in relation to that Ontario Hydro statement was the reaction of the provincial minister, Mr. Norton, who emphasized that it was the intention of the Ontario government to work with other provincial governments and the federal government in bringing forward proposals for the achievement of emission reductions in eastern Canada of 50 per cent by the end of this decade and that that could very well lead to more restrictive limitations on the actions of Ontario Hydro than are presently envisaged.
One favourable consequence of the event the hon. gentleman has discussed has been the underlining of the statement of the provincial environment minister that he is determined to work out effective emission reductions over the next few months, and that Ontario Hydro may very well be required by the provincial government in those circumstances to have even lower emissions than Ontario Hydro now believes we will face.

subtopic: SALARY INCREASE FOR BELL CANADA CHAIRMAN
SALARY INCREASE FOR BELL CANADA CHAIRMAN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, Bell Canada announced yesterday that it would be turning its back on the dream world of 6 per cent and 5 per cent and that it will be going ahead with its plan to increase rates by 25 per cent. Does the minister consider it acceptable for Jean de Grandpre, chairman of Bell Canada, to take a salary increase of 22 per cent, which will bring his annual income to $645,000 a year, and also to ask Canadians to accept 25 per cent increases in their telephone rates?

subtopic: SALARY INCREASE FOR BELL CANADA CHAIRMAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what I said about Mr. Sinclair applies to Mr. Jean de Grandpre also.
I think hon. members should be aware of the way in which the system created by the Minister of Finance and announced in his budget will be implemented. What I say for Bell Canada applies also to Air Canada, for example. Requests for increase in prices will be submitted to regulatory agencies. The regulatory agencies will pass judgments on the validity of those proposed increases. Should approved increases be more than 6 per cent, there is a committee of cabinet which will look at them to find out if they qualify under the theme of extraordinary, exceptional and uncommon circumstances. That is the way the system will be implemented.
Hon. members should not ask each minister each day what he intends to do about CN, Bell and so forth. What we would like to do is let the regulatory system, as it exists now, follow its normal course and act only after decisions have been made by regulatory agencies. It may very well be that in a number of instances the regulatory agencies will not allow more than 6 per cent.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF RESTRAINT TO FAMILY EARNINGS
APPLICATION OF RESTRAINT TO FAMILY EARNINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, Mr. Sinclair, the president of Bell, and the minister who just responded, have said that exceptional increases of more than 6 per cent will be allowed if component costs for organizations like Bell, like Air Canada, and like VIA, are more than 6 per cent. Will Canadian families be allowed to accept increases of more than 6 per cent if their component costs increase by more than 6 per cent?

economic situation of the whole of the air carrier industry. This is the sort of consideration that the committee will have in mind in assessing what are extraordinary circumstances.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSITY STUDENT TUITION FEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State concerning the plight of universities and university students in Canada. The unemployment that affects young persons in Canada is a crushing burden on students who must work to earn tuition fees for next year's university session.
We know that the minister has been talking to the provincial officials responsible for secondary education in Canada and that there has been much discussion, but my question concerns the plight of the university students. Will government funding be so restricted that university students will be faced with tuition increases of 30 per cent and more in the next academic year? I would like the minister to make a commitment to university students now that they will be brought into the world of 6 per cent with respect to tuition fees for the next academic session.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: UNIVERSITY STUDENT TUITION FEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can only begin by complimenting the hon. member for his idea, although the authority to restrict the amount of tuition increase rests with the provinces rather than with the federal government. I think he has struck home at a very, very real concern. I can assure him, through you, Madam Speaker, that the Government of Canada is not going to decrease the amount of money that goes through the provinces for the
July 22, 1982

universities in the coming year, but, rather, is going to increase it by a substantial amount.
This is a matter that I have already been considering, but in view of the hon. member's question I am going to contact the provincial ministers of education further to our meeting on July 9 and urge them to speak to all universities and seek their agreement to limiting any increase in tuition fees to not more than 6 per cent.

Madam Speaker, 1 do not want to add to federal-provincial conflict, but the Secretary of State knows very well that any failure to fund by provincial and federal governments has to be made up by students, through tuition fees. I should like to ask the minister what he meant in his recent press release when he said that the government is moving to strengthen support for students and to improve accessibility to universities. What proposal does the minister have in mind to make it easier for university students to get into university and pay the costs when they get there?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first of all the hon. member is referring to statements that came out of the very productive and friendly meeting that I had with the ministers of education on July 9. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, July 21, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-125, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to Committee of the Whole.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as a result of the efforts of the Progressive Conservative Party, there has been a victory for the people of this nation today, albeit a small one. It should be recognized there has been a victory because this bill, which it should not have been necessary to bring in, asking this country to cough up another $11 billion, has been reduced by $4 billion. The amount is astonishing in itself, but the fact that the government is asking the

July 22, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
people of this nation to come up with that sort of money is absolutely and totally unacceptable.
However, it must be noted that the government recognized that it could not get away with this one in the face of the opposition which has been mounted by this party, in the face of the determination of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), of our House leader and all the critics in this party who have fought so valiantly to ensure that the protection of the people of Canada was first and foremost and was looked after in this House. That particular opposition was launched, initiated and designed by this party. There can be no question but that if we had not taken the initiative and had not shown our determination in the face of the wanton spending habits of the government, the people of Canada, the citizens of this nation, would have had to bear an additional $4 billion in debt. This bill, although I certainly cannot support it, will no doubt be passed by the government majority and the people of the nation will be faced with the burden of an additional $7 billion.
Five weeks ago I stood before the House and debated Bill C-11, which asked for supplementary borrowing authority for only $6.6 billion. Today I am debating the government's request for about that same amount again, plus an additional billion dollars. As old C. D. Howe once asked, "What's a million?" It seems the government has now translated that question into, "What's a billion?"
The government is asking for another $7 billion in borrowing authority. This request means that the government has now asked for a total of $13.6 billion in borrowing authority in the past month, a total of $17.2 billion in borrowing authority for this year, and $39 billion in the two years that it has been in government thus far. Not so long ago, only last November, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stood before the House and advised Canadians of a strategy his government had devised to combat inflation and the recession, a program of economic restraint, equity and renewal. Last month the minister again stood before the House and advised Canadians that we must now strive for economic renewal under the weight of a staggering economic burden, a deficit almost twice the amount expected, a deficit of almost $20 billion. The minister confessed action "must be taken within the very limited room for manoeuvre imposed by the deficit. Recession has resulted in a serious worsening of the government's financial position. Tax revenues have fallen while expenditures have risen". In two short sentences, the minister informed Canadians that the projected budgetary deficit for the current fiscal year will be $19.6 billion instead of the $10.5 billion that he initially projected last November. Our financial requirements are now projected at $17.1 billion instead of the November forecast of $6.6 billion.
In a following paragraph, the Minister of Finance assured us not to worry, for his "last budget put in place a structure of revenues and expenditures that should, when recovery gets fully under way, gradually lower the deficit and avoid putting excessive pressures on capital markets as private borrowing picks up to finance investment". There are no assurances in this statement for a public or an investment community
obliged to deal in an environment of non-confidence in the government or its policies.
In the Progressive Conservative report of the special committee on the budget and the economy, our primary recommendation for economic revitalization was to restore individual and investor confidence by establishing a climate for growth, development and expansion. A Progressive Conservative government would start from the premise that government's role is to accept and enforce an economic framework upon which private individuals and businesses can act with confidence in the future. The current low level of confidence in the future of Canada, combined with high federal spending, are major factors in our current economic situation. It seems that the government is determined to descend upon the people of this country, the taxpayers of this nation, 23 million citizens, like a bunch of screaming banshees out of the heavens, falling on a waiting prey. There seems to be no end to their insatiable desire to spend.
Oftentimes I am asked a question, and I am glad to have the opportunity to set my answer on record. I am asked, "What would you fellows do if you were the government?" For the benefit of those who have asked me that question in the past and for the benefit of those who may ask me in the future but, more particularly, for the benefit of those hon. members opposite who might be genuinely concerned about the deficit imposed by the government on the taxpayers of our country, let me just tell them what a Progressive Conservative government, when elected, will do and would do now if it were in power.
The latest budget came out on June 28. We are led to believe that there will be another budget some time in the fall. It is hard to say just what that might project. I would be very pleased but astonished if the projected deficit by that time had not increased another $4 billion or $5 billion.
Let me state what a Progressive Conservative government would have done had it been in power. First, it would have completely withdrawn the November budget which the Minister of Finance brought in. He seems to have some sort of magical hold on his leader. He remains in office even though he should have gone the way of the grey goose. We would have demonstrated leadership and restraint by holding government spending to the rate of growth in the economy to bring down the deficit. No business enterprise in the nation or in the free world could possibly exist with the kind of financial guidelines under which this government operates. It spends far in excess of what it brings in. It seems to rely on the fact that it still has credit, although I suspect it must be dwindling as quickly as the popularity of this government, which is now in a minus state.
We would have encouraged Canadians to invest by providing incentives. We would have reinstated the small business development bond for small business to allow it to expand. We would not have brought in a disaster plan that is available only
July 22, 1982

to those on the last thread of their rope. We would have put in place a meaningful small business development bond such as we proposed when we were in power.
We would have provided a tax incentive system to give Canadians the opportunity to own their own homes. The minister brought in a program which will offer first-time buyers $3,000 assistance after the first of the year. That is fine. It may be one of the more positive aspects of that budget. However, we should be addressing ourselves to the fact that high mortgage and interest rates are prohibiting young people from purchasing homes in this country. They should be given assistance with their mortgage payments, not the initial amount. Anyone who has the money required to maintain and sustain those rates of interest probably is not as much in need of a $3,000 grant as some of those who should be in homes.
We would have made fundamental changes to the National Energy Program to make it fair to consumers, the provinces and Canadian energy companies. We would have streamlined the Foreign Investment Review Agency to make job-creating foreign investment again welcome in this country.
The deficit brought in by this government is unmanageable and will not earn the confidence of the public or the investment community. National and international investors are leery of this government. It has not only lost control of its spending but has miscalculated its debt by an astounding 100 per cent. What private business or household could survive if it miscalculated its expenditures by almost 100 per cent? It is absolutely astounding. These people are supposed to be responsible. We have seen them for what they are, incompetent rather than competent.
The public does not have confidence in this government today. It does not have confidence in the Minister of Finance or any others in this government who are in a position to make decisions. Members opposite know that. Daily I receive correspondence to this effect. I would just like to read some of these comments which I receive in my office. One states:
I would like for the Prime Minister and his followers to sit at my table for one week, just so they could understand how us poor folks live.
I suspect one day would do. Another reads:
Mr. MacEachen's decision to present a new budget on the p.m. of June 28 should be interesting. I don't hold much hope for any measures which will do anything significant to turn things around.
That was obviously written before the budget. How accurate that person's judgment was! There was nothing significant to turn anything around. The only significant thing was that the government had no alternative but finally to confess that we were in much worse shape than the people of this country were led to believe. Another comment reads:
I am most concerned about the outlook the federal government has taken toward the future of our fair country.
Another one reads:
I would encourage the federal government to withdraw altogether and all go to the Falklands.
That is probably one of the best places they could go. Finally, another constituent writes:
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
Isn't it about time the people of Canada had a chance regarding their future? Please help us.
That is a sad tale. It is a plea for help. Time after time this party has attempted in this House to bring the government to its senses with respect to its spending program and the plight of Canadians. Unfortunately, it always falls on deaf ears.
In my part of the country, Atlantic Canada, all kinds of situations have developed which can be described as nothing less than abusive. This government has made the decision to close CFB Chatham-Newcastle-Miramichi region. That will put 3,500 people out of work and take out of circulation a payroll of $30 million annually. When that closure takes effect, 45 to 50 per cent of the work in that region will become unemployed.
If there was a logical reason or some justification for closing that air force base, 1 could understand the government trying to shore up its effectiveness, but that is not the case. That air base is strategically located in about the best spot it could be for the identification of foreign aircraft. There are foreign aircraft within this country's identification zone. Soviet Bear aircraft have been identified flying through the Canadian identification zone. Those sightings have been made by interceptor aircraft out of CFB Chatham. They are there. We should be in a position to use that base, which is strategically located, and have it continue to play its very vital role. For some reason far beyond my comprehension or the comprehension of those who will be thrown on the unemployment insurance rolls, the new F-18 aircraft is going to be located in Bagotville in the province of Quebec.
Every once in a while it is brought to our attention that perhaps we should not be questioning why all these things which seem to be positive are happening in the province of Quebec, but we are motivated to ask about them because it seems that time and time again the province of Quebec is the recipient of things other provinces traditionally have had. Certainly we must all work together and contribute to the betterment and the building of this nation, but should we not be equitable in our approach to the entire business of economic growth? That is something at which we as parliamentarians and as Canadians should take a serious look. We should want to strive for unity in a way that is beneficial to all of us and in a way that is fair, and surely the best way to do that is to ensure that all Canadians, including Atlantic Canadians, Quebecers, Ontarians and Canadians in the west, get a fair share of the pie.
What happens? We see the closure of CFB Chatham. That does nothing to contribute to unity or an understanding by people who live in Atlantic Canada of problems in other parts of Canada.
We heard in the news this morning that the Heath-Steele mine in northern New Brunswick is being closed down. That is not too far from CFB Chatham. Five hundred people will be thrown out of work. Five hundred people will lose their jobs because of the closure of that mine. That is a result of a poor

July 22, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
and depressed economy. Hon. members opposite are partially responsible for that, and they have to accept their fair share of the blame.
We see that an electronic manufacturing plant in the Moncton region has been delayed by several months. One thousand people, apparently, will be employed, if that plant ever does come on stream. Eight thousand unemployed people put in applications for those potential 1,000 jobs.
We have seen the price of gasoline increase. We have seen VIA Rail services cut and slashed, particularly in New Brunswick. This has happened in Nova Scotia to a lesser degree, but the train which served the southern portion of New Brunswick and gave us our link to Montreal has been cut and hundreds of jobs have been lost. That should never have happend. That train was one of the most used trains, one of the most efficient trains and certainly one of the most popular and best trains in the nation. That train should never have been taken off, yet for some unexplained reason it was. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) will not give us an explanation. The Senate committee has taken him to task and has thoroughly thumped him over this particular arbitrary decision to cut that rail service. The Progressive Conservative task force which travelled across the nation receiving briefs on the discontinuance of VIA Rail lines heard time and time again that people should have had the opportunity to be heard and that the due process should have been followed. We were told that the CTC should have had the opportunity to conduct public hearings. But no, this uncaring, thoughtless and certainly unthankful minister, with the backing of his cabinet colleagues, arbitrarily discontinued that train.
The port of Saint John is a wonderful port, thanks to contributions by the provincial government which has spent about $22 million in recent years on the modernization of that port. There is a grain elevator at that port. We have all the necessary facilities. When Montreal opens up in the summer, we naturally lose business to Montreal. It was not too long ago that I was petitioned by a group of dock workers in Saint John. The petitioners were members of the United Transportation Union in Saint John. They asked me to speak to the minister responsible for grain shipments and to ask if just two or three shipments of wheat or grain could be diverted to the port of Saint John during slow months. They were not asking for a lot but just for a very few. I said I would contact the minister and, indeed, I did. I wrote to the minister on May 25, 1982. That was a month and a half ago, and to date I have not received so much as the courtesy of a reply.
That does not necessarily astound me. Some time ago I asked the minister a question in the House concerning alternate transportation for peole who would be inconvenienced because of the VIA Rail cutbacks. He referred to something about alternate means. He said that if I would give him a list of the communities involved, he would get back to me. I wrote the names of the communities down on a piece of paper and passed them to the minister. He said, "I will get back to you". That was months ago and, of course, I have never heard another word from him. I heard the minister in the House
today answer an hon. member who asked a question of importance to that hon. member. The minister said that if he had received notice, he would have been able to look into the matter and have the answer available. However, the minister said he would look into the matter. Unless the minister is motivated to do something by some sort of attack in the House, I doubt very much if the hon. member will ever hear from the minister.
Let me get back to the matter of grain shipments through the port of Saint John. I asked for only two or three shipments. In the process of all this, 1 contacted the manager of the Saint John port development commission in Saint John and asked him if he would support me in this effort. He wrote back to me because he was concerned, unlike-obviously-the Minister of Transport, who is responsible in this House for the Wheat Board. The manager of the Saint John port development commission was concerned and brought to my attention the fact that he had made representations, along with the port authority, time and time again for this sort of thing to happen. He informed me that when employees at the grain elevators on the St. Lawrence River were on strike back in the summer of 1980-there are four grain elevators in Montreal-he pointed out to the Wheat Board that the grain elevator at Saint John was only partly full and could handle grain quite nicely. He informed the Wheat Board that the port of Saint John would be prepared to take grain and, indeed, invited the Wheat Board to ship grain through the port of Saint John. He was advised that no ships were being nominated for the port of Saint John. The only satisfaction he received from the Wheat Board was that the Wheat Board thanked him for his telephone call. That sort of attitude is intolerable. I do not quite understand why Saint John should be singled out to have its rail services cut, why the government refuses to recognize the $22 million investment of the province of New Brunswick in that port and why the government refuses to divert wheat shipments to that port.
Oddly enough, the core of the city of Saint John is represented in this House by a Liberal member. That member supports the government on every measure. He votes with the government when it wants to cut VIA Rail. He supports the government. He supports the budget. He supports increases in the price of gasoline. He has supported every measure which has come before this House, even those which have been dastardly and have worked against the best interests of the people of Saint John. The hon. member never balks. He never says anything contrary to the government. He always moves in the direction he is told. One would think the government would give this fellow a chance to do something good for his city. One would think the government would throw him a few crumbs once in a while in the form of some assitance for the city of Saint John, but the government totally ignores the poor fellow.
I think it is a crying shame that the hon. member has been forgotten and cast aside. He certainly must be making representations to the government to do something for the people of Saint John. I know that must be taking place, but 1 feel the government is ignoring it. That is a shame, Mr. Speaker.
July 22, 1982

When it comes to members from New Brunswick, there is the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) who sits in this House on many occasions. He has dealt the commercial salmon fishermen of the Saint John region in New Brunswick one of the most severe blows possible; he has cut back their quota for the year. He imposed quotas on fishermen in the Saint John, New Brunswick area which he refused to impose on others in the Atlantic region who fish for the same species. He has imposed on New Brunswick a hardship that he has not the intestinal fortitude to impose on others.
It is difficult to say why this is so. New Brunswick was one of the prime movers in the salmon conservation effort in the early 1970s and voluntarily imposed a ban on commercial salmon fishing. Commercial fishermen had to suffer for that. Most of the slamon caught commercially in the Atlantic region is caught off the coast of Newfoundland. Approximately 65 per cent of those salmon are headed back to their native rivers in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
You do not get to the root of a problem by attempting to solve it at the end; you have to go to the beginning of the problem. It must be recognized by the minister that it is in the best interest of Newfoundlanders, New Brunswickers and Nova Scotians to have total management of the salmon stock in Atlantic Canada, but for some inexplicable reason he chose to cut down on the commercial salmon fishery and angling in New Brunswick. It is worth noting that the tourist industry, the outfitters and guides of New Brunswick, receive a substantial portion of their living and that the province benefits substantially from people who come there for sport salmon fishing.
In depression times people used to be able to go into the woods and saw logs or cut pulp, but the building supply business in New Brunswick is collapsing today. Saw mills are idle and pulp mills are purchasing limited quantities. People do not have the opportunity now to go to the woods and cut pulp in order to feed their families.
In the House today the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) made a great deal of the fact that the government is going to bring Alberta oil to the Atlantic region. This will be subsidized at $2.50 per barrel. If the government had taken a responsible attitude toward the development of energy in the country, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia could be selfsufficient in energy today or could be well on the way to it.
But where is the natural gas pipeline the government promised to build? I understand that the prime contractor and others interested in that pipeline cannot find out when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources intends to bring forth that promised $40 million for the front-end engineering costs of the pipeline. The government made this commitment; there is no two ways about that. The money was promised a long time ago but it is not forthcoming. There has been tinkering and tom-foolery to the point of exasperation. If I were a betting person I would say that the pipeline would never
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
get across the St. Lawrence River as long as the minister is in office.
The government is spending money on taxis. It spent $3.5 million on taxis last year. The Department of Transport alone spent $422,000 of that. The government spent $16.7 million on telegrams. I could go on and on about the way the government wastes the money of the Canadian taxpayer but I do not have too much time left.
Let us consider who are the big losers in this program. Sadly enough, they include the single taxpayer, all taxpayers without children and married taxpayers with children who earn more than $12,000 per year. The cruelest blow of all is to the senior citizens drawing old age security who have to rely on that and perhaps a little bit of supplemental income from investments. These people suffer the most because of the ineptitude of the government. I have no time for a government that chooses to ruin the country on the backs of the old age pensioners. The people of this country have no time for that sort of government either. It has deindexed everything. That means that inflation is in the interests of the government; it will receive more in tax revenue because inflation is on its side. That is not an incentive, it is a disincentive.
This program may in the short term bring in a few more dollars but it will backfire on the government. It is going to force so many people out of work in this country that there will be fewer and fewer people in a position to pay taxes.
The social programs that have been so generous in the past will have to bear a greater burden. We should have been putting money aside for a rainy day. No lifetime goes by without its share of rainy days, but the government did not recognize that. It chose to fool the people into thinking it had good managers and was in charge of the situation. It was in charge of opening the purse strings and losing every last nickel we had. From the way members of the government strut around you would think they were proud of that.
The government seems to have been determined to carry through with its policies, knowing full well what is bound to happen to it within the foreseeable future. It is almost as though it has adopted a scorched earth policy and is going to level everything. It is going to make sure that whoever gets into power-and there is no question about that the next time around; we will be there and we will have to clean up the mess, but we will deal with it and deal with it effectively. But the government is not going to give us much of a chance when it is forced finally to turn over the reins of government in this nation.
The Minister of Finance has stated that he now anticipates our deficit to be in the vicinity of $19.6 billion, up about $10.1 billion from what it was projected to be last November. 1 issue a challenge to the Minister of Finance here in the House. If by the end of the fiscal year the deficit goes over $19.6 billion by, say, just $2 billion-I could have said $1 billion or one penny-the only alternative-I will not say "the only honourable thing" because there is no honour left in that bunch over

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words this afternoon on Bill C-125, one of the bills flowing from the budget. As we begin to participate in this debate our country, along with all other western industrialized countries, faces one of the most difficult times since the 1930s. It is a time when over 30 million people in the OECD countries are unemployed, and we are especially concerned about the 1.25 million unemployed in Canada.
Although the figures in the budget documents indicate that Canada had one of the highest levels of growth in 1981, it is projected to have one of the strongest declines in 1982. The interesting aspect of that, Mr. Speaker, is that most of the growth in 1981 occurred during the first half, certainly during the first three-quarters of the year. In fact, we went into a sharp decline in the third and fourth quarter of 1981, and of course that is projected to continue this year. So the impact on unemployment in this country is much worse than it would have been otherwise.
The other interesting fact, I think an alarming one and one which concerns us a great deal, is that the decline in growth in the United States is second only to Canada, that being a 1.6 per cent decline from 1981. The United States being our largest trading partner, this is very significant for us. High interest rates in the United States, compared to their inflation rate, have driven down the value of the currencies of all western industrialized countries relative to the U.S. In 1981 the Canadian dollar rose marginally less than 1 per cent against the U.S. dollar, while all other currencies declined sharply. For example, West Germany declined by 12.4 per cent, the U.K. by 19.9 per cent, the Japanese by 7.3 per cent, and the French by 20.7 per cent. This decline has continued into 1982. The Canadian dollar, at the time of the budget, had declined by 7.8 per cent, whereas all other major western currencies had declined by larger amounts.
A few nights ago I was surprised and very concerned about a report on the CBC national news that much of the decline in the value of the Canadian dollar was due to the fact that many of the large chartered banks and financial institutions were investing large portions of their funds in U.S. securities. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very harmful thing for us, although many of us from resource areas in Canada do not really mind seeing a lower dollar because it means our exports of natural resources bring a better return in Canada. However, it does have an inflationary effect on our economy.
This is a time when the banks are pressing small-business men, farmers, fishermen and home owners almost unmercifully by calling loans and so on. At a time when they are charging very high interest rates, this seems most inappropriate. At the same time many chartered banks are closing rural branches. For example, in my constituency, in the community of Manito-waning on Manitoulin Island, there has been a branch of the Bank of Montreal for the last 75 years. The community has a
stable population and the branch serves several thousand people. The next nearest branch is 25 to 30 miles away in an adjoining community. There are many senior citizens living there who do not have transportation. The second largest Indian band in the province of Ontario with over 2,000 resident band members is immediately adjacent.
The bank is working at full tilt with a staff of seven and apparently a need for more people, but they informed the reeve and the councillors a few weeks ago that they plan to shut down this branch in the next several weeks. They complain about many problems, such as too many branches, some bad debts and perhaps poor administration, yet instead of the bank absorbing the costs involved at a time of record high interest rates and record high profits during the past year, they are leaving the local residents to suffer. It seems to me that with this kind of patriotism shown by Canada's chartered banks we do not really need any traitors in this country.
It seems clear, Mr. Speaker, from examining the world economy and the loss of growth projected for the U.S. and many other countries, as outlined in the budget document, that the world demand for many commodities is going to be very poor this year. Not only that, but prices are going to be very low. In fact, during the past three or four months the price of some minerals like copper has been proportionately lower than in the 1930s in the depths of the depression. For those of us living in resource areas like northern Ontario which produce commodities like nickel, copper, uranium, pulp and paper, steel and so on, this is a bad omen for the prospect of any dramatic upturn in the economy during the coming year.
There is very little that Canada can do to pull the international markets of the world out of a recession. However, in my own constituency, a large number of megaprojects are still under construction. The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) spoke about the need for incentives. In fact, there have been very strong incentives for many industries. For instance, the steel industry, the pulp and paper industry and others have put in place massive construction projects. In my own constituency many are still going on this year and are providing valuable employment at a time when many of the products being produced are in low demand or their prices are very marginal. In fact, in Espanola at the Eddy forest products plant a construction project is going on now. This construction program has been going on for the past year and will continue for another year. It is worth over $200 million and is to modernize and upgrade the pulp and paper mill. A few years ago a large saw mill was built. This saw mill will produce over one million board feet of lumber per year. That kind of construction and facility in a year of low demand is very beneficial in terms of jobs.
Likewise, in Elliot Lake a massive expansion of the uranium mining operations has taken place. Some of it is still continuing. The final expansion and development of those mines to meet the increasing demand is going on. This year 600 or 700
July 22, 1982

new houses will be constructed providing additional employment during a period of low demand for many of the commodities.
In Blind River a uranium refinery is under construction costing $130 million. This is creating many jobs in that community.
Similarly, a few months ago the federal, provincial and municipal governments in Sault Ste. Marie signed an agreement to spend $70 million on a major community infrastructure program. This will provide new sewer and water facilities for that community to accommodate the growth which is planned for Algoma Steel during the course of this decade. That megaproject will start construction next year and will provide employment at a time when the demand for steel products is down.
During the past couple of years the steel industry in Canada has been going through a major construction period with massive investments of several billions of dollars, some of it at Algoma Steel. The incentives which have been put in place should be continued for this vital industry.
Our steel industry in Canada has fared better than most other steel industries around the world, but ours is suffering now like many other industries because of the economic downturn. However, the steel industry is modernizing, it is competitive and the lower dollar is beneficial in that regard. Its know-how, expertise and its competitive situation are its strongest ally for the future.
If we can put in place programs to modernize and upgrade the pulp and paper industry and the steel industry through a system of incentives, we should do the same for other industries, such as the high technology industry, during the next few years in order to make them competitive and able to meet the challenge in the international community. This will also, of course, provide jobs.
There is not a great deal Canadians can do to pull the world out of recession which all western industrialized nations face right now. It is difficult for us to create more demand. I do believe our trade department and our minister should be continuing their efforts to get out and fight for the markets that are available. We should have incentives and programs to assist in that regard.
What is worrisome in the international statistics presented in the budget is the rate of inflation in Canada as compared to the United States, our principal trading partner and our strongest market. The inflation rate for May stood at 11.8 per cent in Canada, whereas it was 6.7 per cent in the United States. At the same time our wage settlements were running something like 5 per cent above those of our best customer, the United States of America. Therefore, our concern must be not only with the unemployed, but with assisting small business, home owners, fishermen and the farmers, and we must take action to increase our productivity of those commodities we produce and manufacture in this country. We must produce efficiently and our products must be at a price at which they can be sold in international markets.
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
International trade is very important to Canada. It is perhaps more important to us than to any other country in the world. Something like 30 per cent of our GNP comes from international trade and for many of our rural and northern areas, it is the principal source of income and employment. I believe that is why the government has proposed in the budget papers and the budget bills that we set as a target the reduction of our inflation rate to 6 per cent next year and to 5 per cent the following year. These are not targets for inflation picked out of a hat or grasped out of thin air; they are goals we must achieve if in the next two years we want to be competitive in the real world where our products are sold and if we want to be on a par with the United States in selling the products of our factories, our forests and our mines. Sure enough, the world economy and the demand for products will turn around, but the question is whether our inflation rate will drive our production costs to a height where we will no longer be able to compete or sell abroad.
I know that the opposition parties and some companies have indicated their opposition to the proposals of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Perhaps that is not surprising since they are sworn to oppose the government in every way possible. It seems to me the opposition from Bell Canada and Air Canada to a program to reduce prices to a 6 per cent ceiling is not satisfactory. This morning The Globe and Mail carried an article under the heading "Bell, Air Canada set to challenge 6 per cent prices limit". It seems to me most of the people in this country really want to reduce the inflation rate to 6 per cent and 5 per cent during the next two years. As the world comes out of the current recession, people want us to be in a position to compete and to seize markets.
The rather unfortunate part of all this is that companies such as Air Canada and Bell Canada are almost in monopoly positions. Air Canada has some competition with CP and a few other companies, but Bell Canada has practically no competition. It has a virtual monopoly. I think many people are becoming fed up with the ever-increasing demand for 25 per cent or whatever every year or so. Even a 6 per cent increase will be very high for low-income Canadians, senior citizens and those who are out of work.
I have opposed practically every rate increase Bell Canada has put forward to the CRTC during the last three or four years, but much of my opposition was due to its very poor service. My argument before the CRTC was that if Bell Canada wanted massive increases, then let it provide improved services to rural areas, extended calling areas and so on. In this case I certainly oppose its request for an increase because 1 think it is in the national interest for Canadians to work together toward the goal of 6 per cent and 5 per cent for the next two years. I believe Bell Canada should support such a national program. It seems to me that if the CRTC does not bring Bell Canada into line to support the program, then surely the government should do it.

July 22, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
A Crown corporation the size and magnitude of Air Canada, with its great impact upon Canadian transportation costs, should fall in line with and support the program. I know there is a mechanism in place for its application to go to the CTC, but it seems to me that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) should call a meeting of the shareholders of Air Canada. The Minister of Transport should lay the facts of life before Mr. Taylor, the president of Air Canada. There are many people out there hurting. There are senior citizens who cannot afford an increase in transportation costs of 6 per cent or over. There are businessmen and farmers who will also be affected because they have to make necessary business trips. There are many unemployed people in the same position. The minister should ask the president of Air Canada to co-operate and, if he says no, he should be advised that the shareholders held a meeting and he was voted out of office. If he does not want to cooperate in this program, there are many people awaiting his position.
This program is largely a voluntary one. There are regulations through the CTC, the CRTC and other federal regulatory agencies. There is control in the bill which is now before committee concerning federal public servants and employees of Crown corporations. If average Canadians see large, powerful companies such as Bell Canada and Air Canada not cooperating, the chances of obtaining co-operation and assistance from them will be very difficult.
I am impressed by the real amount of co-operation I have seen on the policy. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has met with the provincial premiers. There seems to be a good rapport and there has been good response. I understand that further meetings are planned. All of these things are very encouraging. Also the response from the meeting with the CLC and other trade union groups seemed very encouraging. Further meetings will be taking place there.
Likewise there has been a very good response from business. For example, yesterday a group of senior businessmen talked about how they could work together and co-operate to reduce the inflation rate, to increase our productivity and to bring in, over the next couple of years, a policy or a program which will place Canada in a good position when there is a turnaround in the world recession and a return to a growth situation.
Within the last three or four weeks a number of companies have indicated their support for the program. They are planning to co-operate. I am referring to companies such as Alcan, Cominco, General Foods, Heritage Group, Hiram Walker, Polysar, Sherritt-Gordon and White Farm. Many more have indicated that they want to support the program. Also there has been a great deal of support from individual Canadians.
I should like to read a letter which I received from a constituent. This person wrote:
This letter is with reference to our economic situation. First of all I am in support of the 6 per cent guidelines, essentially. However, I feel much more is needed in order to cure our economic difficulties as follows:
(a) A coalition government as I believe any reasonable ideas re our situation
economically should be acted upon
(b) establish a "social" contract with our members of the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association or Chamber of Commerce. This "social" contract would be similar to West Germany's system which has worked considerably better than our present adversary system. I do realize part of the problem would have to be addressed provincially. However, my philosophy is one of tripartism. That is, government, business and labour must work together. Legislation would have to be changed.
The letter continued:
(d) Let us promote a new era of research and development in Canada.
Overall, I feel that we should adopt an attitude of open mindedness to new solutions rather than an "it will never work in Canada" attitude to economic and other solutions.
There is support from many, many Canadians. They want to see us work together. The kinds of meetings which the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister are attending with the provincial governments, business and industry are supported by many Canadians.
The kind of co-operation we saw in the House today wherein the government varied the amount of the borrowing authority is commendable. We will have two pieces of legislation, if necessary, on the borrowing authority rather than one. The government is protecting its position to raise the required funds for all its social programs during this fiscal year. At the same time it is being sensitive to and considerate of the position of the opposition in regard to giving the government a blank cheque for the fiscal year. This is the kind of commendable co-operation to which my constituent referred.
The budget documents set out a program of co-operation because of our concern for inflation. They also contain a new and innovative proposal for indexed investment certificates where people who invest their money in this new proposed financial instrument would pay income tax only on that part of the interest above the inflation rate. Indeed, this is a new, interesting and perhaps novel idea. 1 am sure that people begrudge paying income tax on interest which, in effect, is only inflation.
At the same time, this new indexed investment certificate would reduce the borrowing cost for development of small business, agriculture, fishing and housing by 3 per cent to 6 per cent. Those are the areas where we want to create investment and provide assistance. If we can accomplish this through this new instrument, I suggest it will be very beneficial.
I think it is significant that this potentially complicated instrument is being referred to a blue ribbon committee of people who are knowledgeable in that field, including representatives from the trade union movement. This will mean that there will be consultation and co-operation with the private sector that will produce a much more workable and practical system.
It has also been proposed that there be a similar instrument for investment by Canadians for equity stock position. I am especially pleased that there is provision in the budget documents for direct employment programs. Many of the rural
July 22, 1982

areas in my constituency which do not have principal industries have very high seasonal unemployment. The direct employment programs work very well in these areas. Not only do they create employment for hard-pressed municipalities every year, but they provide many worthwhile programs. Among these are renovations and improvements to community facilities as well as aiding in the development of the tourist industry through the construction of parks, recreational facilities and marinas in co-operation with groups like the small craft harbours branch, which has been especially active throughout the Algoma-Manitoulin area. Their work has been appreciated very much. I believe that area has the largest number of government wharves and docks of any constituency on the Great Lakes.
There is some $200 million provided in the budget for direct employment programs, another $150 million for employment intensive programs carried out by departments and another $100 million from existing programs in the Canada employment department. This totals some $450 million. As well, there is another $300 million for permanent private incentive programs. This gives a total allocation for employment and direct employment support programs of some $750 million.
There has also been a great deal of funding provided for the housing industry which will create additional jobs for Canadians. I believe the budget projects some 300,000 jobs that will be created by the programs outlined in the budget papers. This includes the direct employment programs, such as the community development program, the labour intensive projects within government departments as well as programs like the forestry worker employment support program which was announced several months ago.
1 think one of the most interesting provisions of the budget was the direct injection of additional money into the housing industry. I hope this money will be put in place as soon as possible in order to proceed with those projects, especially in northern areas where winter construction of foundations and footings is difficult. There is a total of approximately $300 million provided for first-time buyers and builders of houses in the form of $3,000 grants. Similarly, the housing repair program was oversubscribed from the day it was announced a few months ago. That program has doubled.
1 am anxiously awaiting the announcement of the 2,500 additional units of co-operative housing because we have a proposal from the community of Elliot Lake in my constituency where we hope to construct 62 additional units of cooperative housing. This is an innovative program which has great potential. Construction of these units will be a first for the Algoma constituency where most of the housing is provided by the mining companies. There is very little private sector accommodation for people working in the service sector of the community. This will be a valuable addition for them.
All of these programs which were announced in the budget have been very useful. I am especially pleased that there will be approximately $200 million for the agricultural industry to provide low-interest money for farmers who are particularly hard pressed. This money will be provided at 12.5 per cent,
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
which is 4 per cent below the Farm Credit Corporation lending rate, presently 16.5 per cent.
As well, there is the interest reduction funds of some $400 million which will be available to reduce interest rates for small-business men, farmers and fishermen by some 4 per cent for investment in new projects. Elopefully, this additional funding to assist these industries during the next few months will cover that gap until the new investment instrument which I have previously mentioned is put into place.
With the implementation of those projects I believe that much progress has taken place. I believe that the budget addresses many aspects of the problems we face today in our tough economic times. It addresses the question of inflation and introduces a plan to work toward a reduction in inflation during the next two years. It also provides incentives for investment, reduction of interest rates, job-creation programs and improvements to our housing situation. These are a number of items which I believe are important and should receive the support of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to intervene in Bill C-125, an act to provide supplementary borrowing authority. The bill will enable the government to borrow sums of money which it needs to keep the government operating.
I find that there have been some absurdities during the debate. The first occurred yesterday when the Liberals introduced a notice of motion to bring in closure of the debate. At that point, opposition members felt that there were perhaps enough speeches on the record to deal with the borrowing authority bill and so no more hon. members spoke on behalf of the opposition yesterday. So all day yesterday, hon. members in the Liberal Party talked out their own bill and would not allow it to come to a vote. As an individual Member of Parliament, I found that to be very strange indeed.
The next absurdity was that the government, in asking for this borrowing authority, was asking to borrow $11 billion. We found that the government really did not need $11 billion. It was just projecting that times were getting so bad that it may have lost control and that it wanted extra money to provide a cushion, so that it could just run to the lending institutions to borrow extra sums of money.
Then this afternoon we had another absurdity when we heard the government itself admitting that it did not really need to borrow $11 billion, of which the NDP and the Conservatives were aware, so the government introduced a motion to reduce the amount requested in Bill C-125. We will be voting at 9.45 this evening on Bill C-125. The Conservatives were very happy to hear the government say that it was reducing the amount of its borrowing authority bill to $7 billion. However, if the government needs more money by the end of the fiscal year, it can just borrow another $4 billion without further debate.

speechtext:
This session started on April 14, 1980, after the February 18, 1980 general election. Since that time the government has asked for authority to borrow money on four different occasions. First, the government brought forward Bill C-30 and requested authority to borrow $12 billion. Then it came to us with Bill C-59 and asked for borrowing authority for an additional $14 billion. That did not seem to be enough. Bill C-111 was brought forward and the government asked for borrowing authority for an additional $6.6 billion, bringing the total to $32.6 billion up to this point. Even that is not enough. Bill C-125 is now before us and the government is asking for another $11 billion, bringing the grand total since April 14, 1980, when this session started, to some $43.6 billion.
That is only the surface of the problem with the government. By the end of this fiscal year, the accumulated debt of the federal government will be $150 billion, or possibly even more. My home province could run on that amount of money, with present day dollars, for about 75 years.
I think the former Auditor General was quite right when he stated in his annual report that the government has lost control of the public purse. This accumulated national debt puts an increased strain on the economy of the country. It has been created by successive Liberal and Conservative governments which have been unable to deal with the business of running the country. It has also been created by increasing government deficits year after year.
The budget brought down in November by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) projected that the deficit this year would be some $10 billion. Then on June 28, when we found we needed a new budget, the government admitted that it had miscalculated. Even though we all knew we were in bad economic times and that the government had a back-up support staff of some 300,000 or more people to provide information about this country, we found at that time, on June 28, that the deficit had increased by almost twice the amount we were told in November it would be. It had increased to $19.6 billion. That is a large amount of money. There are some other countries throughout the world with larger deficits, such as the United States of America, whose deficit is much larger, but on a per capita basis the deficit in Canada is twice that of the United States of America.
What does a deficit like that mean? From time to time we in the New Democratic Party have advocated deficit budgeting, but the type of deficit budgeting which is needed and can be allowed is very different from the type which is being adopted by the Liberal government and which it is locked into. It is perpetual, year after year, and it gets worse and worse. If there is to be a deficit budget, it would make sense to have deficit budgeting in areas where there can be investment in the future and revenue can be generated for the operation of the country in future years.
I would like to compare our federal deficit to some of the provincial deficits across the country. Using 1978 figures, the source being the Bank of Montreal, the debt in British Columbia under a Social Credit government was $2,497 for every man, woman and child. In great Tory Alberta it was $2,222 for every man, woman and child. In great Ontario it was $2,544. The lowest in Canada was the small province of Prince Edward Island. The next lowest in Canada in 1978 under an NDP government was the province of Saskatchewan. It was $1,709 in that province, much better than any Liberal or Tory administration anywhere in Canada.
There is often talk about the size of bureaucracies. My source of information is Statistics Canada, 1979. In Alberta under that great Tory government which believes in carving off the fat, 2.6 per cent of the population was employed in the public service. At that time in Saskatchewan under an NDP government, it was 1.9 per cent of the population, the lowest in Canada.
The spending of this government places a great load on the Canadian people. It spends at the rate of $214 million a day, which breaks down to $9 million an hour or $150,000 a minute.

I am sure the people in the galleries will listen to these figures even if the members of the House will not. Per capita spending on behalf of every one of you sitting in the gallery in 1967-68 was $549 for every man, woman, child and baby in this country. For the 1982-83 fiscal year, that amount has increased to $3,175 for every single one of you in the gallery. Compare this to some of the municipal governments. Maybe some responsibility should be placed on them because
July 22, 1982

they may be better able to handle it. In places like The Batt-lefords-Meadow Lake the per capita spending today is in the area of $570 or $580 for every man, woman and child.
When you look at the situation for taxpayers, Mr. Speaker, it is even worse. Many do not pay taxes because they are unemployed. Others do not pay taxes because they are retired and do not have a large enough income to require them to pay taxes. However, each and every taxpayer in the 1982-83 fiscal year will have to pay $8,251. With increasing unemployment and a worsening economy, this figure will ever increase. In fact, the debt in Canada will soon take in excess of 30 per cent of all the money the government raises in revenue just to service the debt. That is a shameful state of affairs.
This great amount of money has very serious effects on the interest rates that individual Canadians have to pay to financial institutions. There are a couple of things that happen. Either the government prints more money, which is inflationary, or it takes huge sums out of the money supply in this country. The more competition there is for money, the more interest rates are forced up. With this government taking some $150 billion out of the economy, it causes great upward pressure on interest rates.
It is not only government spending which does that. Throughout the world huge sums of money are spent each year on armaments. Each year $500 billion is spent on armaments throughout the world. This has a very harmful effect on the money supply and affects those who have to borrow for their mortgages or small businesses. The money is just not available. It is said that the way to get into small business in Canada today is to buy a big business, vote Liberal or Conservative, and then sit back and wait because it will soon be a small business.
The purpose of the government is to govern in areas where individuals cannot operate as effectively and efficiently with due regard for economy, in a manner that is fair and equitable to all people. The problem is that this government has lost control.
It is not just the public or private sector, but a problem of magnitude, how large and overbalanced this government has become. We must attempt to turn that around. It is also a problem of magnitude in the private sector and the public sector. I point to the problems experienced in the last few years by Massey-Ferguson, Ford, Chrysler and other huge companies not now as effective and prosperous as they once were.
What are some of the alternatives? Eventually we in this country will have to get away from the centralist attitude. I say this as an individual Member of Parliament. The small constituencies in Canada must become more self-sufficient. The local people should have more input. The members of the Conservative Party are having a great laugh during my speech in the House of Commons. I find it strange that the NDP are often blamed for some of the ills in this country, yet we have never formed a federal government since confederation in 1867. We have influenced and helped to bring in many good
International Development Research Centre
programs, but the blame lies nowhere else than on successive Conservative and Liberal regimes in this country.
With regard to smaller areas gaining self-sufficiency, the local people would feel much better if they had control over their own destiny. Members of Parliament are often frustrated because of their lack of input and the fact that this government often will not listen.
