The House resumed, from Thursday, June 10, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stewart:
That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all communications, transcripts or notes of interviews, memos, notes of telephone conversations, applications for grants, bursaries and fellowships between the government through the International Development Research Centre and any other person or group requesting or being considered for financial grants from the International Development Research Centre, particularly relating to financial grants or fellowships or financial sponsorship to individuals who hold or held elected or appointed office in governments of other countries or who were or are members of recognized political parties in other foreign nations.

Mr. Speaker, because of a particular situation in the House on June 10, debate on this motion was shortened, so I thank you again for giving me the opportunity to finish the remarks which I began on that day.
The motion under consideration is a motion regarding Canada's role in international aid, with particular reference being made to the International Development Research Centre. The motion was introduced by the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart). In his remarks at the opening of debate that day he criticized-unfairly, I felt-Canada's aid program for those parts of the world which need help at this particular time. The argument he used was simply that when times are tough in Canada, we should think of ourselves first and other people when times get better. I do not hold to that principle, simply because the aid program Canada has is a program which, as well as helping people in the Third World, also helps Canadians. Eighty per cent of the aid given by Canada remains here. Because it is given in a tied form, the money which is given in the form of aid is used to buy materials here in Canada.

July 22, 1982
International Development Research Centre
The motion directs itself particularly to the International Development Research Centre here in Ottawa, which is a small group receiving about 3 per cent of the aid budget of Canada. However, I feel that the work done by this centre amounts to far more than 3 per cent of our total aid program. Throughout its history, I believe the International Development Research Centre has shown that this kind of aid given in this particular way helps bring about results in the developing world and in Canada as well. The results produced by the centre far outweigh the money spent.
An editorial in the Cape Breton Post of April 3 of this year gives a very positive outlook on the work of the International Development Research Centre, and I would just like to read from that editorial as follows:
The annual review of Canada's International Development Research Centre affords a textbook example of the way to go about helping the unfortunates of the impoverished Third World. Instead of making magniloquent talk about "global negotiations" and "the Spirit of Cancun," this unobtrusive federal agency goes about sponsoring a myriad of relatively inexpensive programs aimed at applying scientific knowledge toward heightening the quality of life.
Since its formation in 1970 the Centre has been concentrating on supporting researchers living and working in developing regions and on other research to promote the well-being of the rural poor of the semi-arid tropics. Their crying needs are food, energy, clean water and sanitation which in our blessed abundance we here tend to take for granted. Yet, as the IDRC points out, simply acquiring enough of these occupies one-third of the world's people, all day, every day. To fail to do so is to fail to survive.
The tone of that editorial is very close to the direction taken by the parliamentary task force on North-South relations, on which I happened to have the privilege to serve last year. All three parties in this House were represented on that task force, and the task force presented the same basic idea about aid. That idea is that aid is not something which deprives but something which really does build an economic base for people to develop themselves. I would just like to read from page 12 of our report as follows:
Investment (not charity) in the well-being of the poor is frequently the best economic investment a country or the world can make. A small farmer with education raises his yields dramatically. A mother with decent nutrition can nurse healthy children who can learn and work more productively.
Robert McNamara, a former minister of defence of the United States and a former president of the World Bank- certainly anything but a left-wing socialist in his basic thinking-has observed:
It used to be said that lack of capital was the chief obstacle to economic growth. But we now know that capital formation explains less than one-third of the variations in growth rates among developing countries; human resource development explains a great deal more. Investment in the human potential of the poor, then, is not only morally right, it is very sound economics.
Coming from Robert McNamara, a former president of the World Bank, I say that is something which should be taken with no grain of salt.
Our report continued:
The lesson is being learned. The International Development Strategy for the 1980s, recently approved at the Special Session of the United Nations, gives concrete expression to the philosophy of investment in the poor. It contains specific goals and objectives relating to the elimination of hunger, universal primary education, primary health care for all and a sharp reduction in infant
mortality by the end of the century. In particular the role of women in development and the need to integrate them into all the sectors of development has been fully recognized.
It is with those thoughts and in those terms that I would like to draw my remarks to a close because I realize my time is very limited. I would like to finish by telling of a small incident. I spoke today with a physician friend of mine formerly from Saskatoon and now from St. Boniface, Dr. Ian Carr, who is one of the physicians for social responsibility and has just returned from the Pugwash conference. He spoke to me today, and for the first time I met a person who spoke about the possibility of an impending third world war as being within the timetable of a few months. He spoke of 18 months as being a timetable people who were at Pugwash feel is a probability or a reality in relation to a nuclear world war.
With respect to development, one of the greatest problems is that huge amounts of money are being taken out of the economies of the world and directed to the building of armaments. My colleague, the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish), referred to this. Many of these armaments are now being sent into developing countries with no purpose at all except to destroy. Somehow we, the responsible people on the face of the globe, must take note of this reality. Something must be done to reduce the tensions which bring about war so that everyone will have enough on which to live and so that everyone will have access to health care and the opportunity to be educated. That seems reasonable. Why is it that we cannot find a way to turn the whole armaments movement around? We do not have centuries in which to do this. We should be turning it around within a matter of hours, days, weeks and months, because the inevitable drive of armaments is for destruction.
I hate to finish my remarks on that note, but I think what l said does relate to what is going on. The hon. member for Simcoe South criticized aid programs in his speech. Instead of using aid money to build a human world, money is being used to build armaments for the destruction not just of the first world, the second world and the third world, but the whole world. I think my colleagues here and people everywhere should take this matter very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to participate in this debate and a particular honour to follow my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle), who, as we all know, has dedicated a large part of his life to helping others, mainly the poor people of South America. I am also delighted to follow the distinguished member for Saskatoon East in this debate because he was a recipient under the bursary program of IRDC. That points to another avenue of success for IRDC that makes a lot of countries envy the program launched by the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson in 1971.
I think it would be proper for me to begin my remarks by quoting the president of IRDC, Mr. Ivan Head, who said:
It is shortsighted to assume that North-South relations are played according to the rules of a zero-sum game in which each point gained by one participant is a
July 22, 1982

point lost to another. International development, in fact, is a mutually beneficial process in which all win, or in default of which all lose. The over-all health and vitality of the developing world is central to the well-being of the economically developed nations-
That includes Canada. I believe that those words of wisdom from the president of IRDC mean that we should think about this warning. The hon. member for Saskatoon East brought out the point that aid to a developing country is aid to the donor country, because we make sure that the wealth of the world is better divided.

Mr. Speaker, the philosophy behind the establishment of the International Development Research Centre was to develop and support research throughout the world, and particularly in developing countries, since only 3 per cent of research was being done in those countries. In the eighteenth century, famous scientists such as Lavoisier and Celsius made their contribution to the well-being of the population of this earth, while the nineteenth century had Ampere, Kelvin, Pasteur, Darwin and Doppler, to name only a few. The twentieth century, however, has not seen the same level of research activity in developing countries, and of course far less there than elsewhere. So the philosophy behind the IDRC, Mr. Speaker, was to enable industrialized countries like Canada to make a contribution to research in various fields, with emphasis on nutrition, farming, drinking water supplies, forest protection and so forth. As a result, Mr. Speaker, projects have been designed and implemented by the government and the IDRC, and their success has been the pride of that agency.
Mr. Speaker, with my colleague for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) and others, I have had an opportunity to visit a number of projects in the Philippines, Singapore, and Bangladesh. It was very exciting to see the results of these projects and the impact these research and development activities can have on the economic development and well-being of developing countries. In the Philippines for instance, rice production, in certain areas, had more than tripled, thanks to flood-resistant strains that were developed locally. Similarly, special wheat strains were developed locally for growing during the dry season on the same soil where rice is grown during the rainy season, since in that climate, crops can be grown twelve months a year.
There are research centres that attract researchers from all over the world, because they have been able to provide favourable conditions for their work. Those of us who have had an opportunity to visit Bangladesh will have seen that this country, which so often suffers from typhoons and floods has, in only a few years, with the help of the IDRC, been able to develop special strains of rice and wheat and other agricultural products that are highly weather-resistant, and today, one of the most serious problems facing Bangladesh is a shortage of storage space for rice and wheat. It goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that the activities of our International Development Research Centre have had tangible and extremely useful results for developing countries. At the same time, the IDRC has tried to
International Development Research Centre
meet the needs of countries that are faced with a variety of problems. There are of course Canadians and North Americans who, from their comfortable vantage point, tend to judge people in developing countries rather severely, and who tend to believe programs like W5, for instance, whose staff filmed a horror story about the results of the DRIP project in Haiti. They were not altogether factual or honest in their approach, because they neglected to mention the positive achievements of both CIDA and the IDRC. Mr. Speaker, if people would only look at the facts, they would see how often the IDRC and CIDA have been successful in their activities.
Of course, there is a difference between countries that have to cope with a number of climatic conditions such as typhoons-I was referring just now to Bangladesh which has this problem as well as floods-the droughts in the Sahel, earthquakes and flooding in Nicaragua and hurricanes in the West Indies, Mr. Speaker, there is indeed a difference between these countries and ours and our neighbour to the South, which are blessed with a stable climate and well-defined seasons during which farm production can go on uninterrupted, without the risk of the catastrophes I have just mentioned. Mr. Speaker, that is why the activities of our research centre are so widely supported, and let me remind my colleagues opposite that it was not a minister on this side of the House who, with great verve and eloquence, defended the activities of the IDRC in Vienna in 1979. I am referring to the Hon. Senator Martial Asselin who was talking about the IDRC's activities and its achievements. He used the IDRC as an example of what other industrialized countries could do to provide assistance to developing countries. So this should help to reassure the member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) with respect to the activities of the IDRC and its achievements.
To get back to this horror story that was shown to Canadian television audiences on the W5 program, the film only stressed the administrative problems the project had experienced. For instance, the program showed some fire hydrants, with the comment: How ridiculous to instal fire hydrants in a village like Petit-Goave! Well, Mr. Speaker, it would be ridiculous not to instal fire hydrants, because those people need water and fire protection as much as any Canadian, because their buildings and homes are made of wood. Furthermore, the hydrant is a water station. Since most homes do not have drinking water, people have to go to a water station, and the hydrants are a source of potable water. And as to the comment that it was entirely ridiculous to replace the fire hydrants, they were put there by the Americans in the first place, many years ago, I think in the thirties, for the reasons I just mentioned.
In the same program, an attempt was also made to have Canadians believe that the roads that were built had been and were being used only by project workers. That is absolute nonsense, Mr. Speaker, because we used the road that goes up to the mountains, and besides being used to move equipment

July 22, 1982
International Development Research Centre
and supplies for the construction of the clinic and the technical training school, the road is also there to help people get around, for instance, farmers who have to come down from the mountain with their produce to Petit-Goave, and would otherwise have to go through the valleys along rough paths. The road is built and it will be around for a long time because it has not been eroded by rainfall. It is maintained by the people of Petit-Goave, and it is used by area farmers and the people in charge of the medical clinic and the school, so the people are really motivated to maintain the road.
There was also the issue of irrigation projects. Here again, Mr. Speaker, the program would have Canadians believe-and after all, why shouldn't they, since they are paying for the project through their taxes-that the irrigation project was useless since it had to be redone. Now I am sorry, but we visited this project, and I think the whole story was a fantasy, because the project is going to improve the irrigation of arable land in the area concerned, while it will not require a lot of maintenance and repairs since there is very little soil erosion in that particular area. My point, Mr. Speaker, is that all this almost obscene talk about the complete or almost complete failure of certain projects is certainly not conducive to making Canadians understand the need and the urgency for continuing projects that have been undertaken in order to help developing countries.
Of course, not everything went according to plan, and we must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that carrying out an integerated project in a country like Haiti with its particular political climate is quite different from what it would be in Canada. We were so ambitious and so eager to get on with it, and 1 am referring to our CIDA officers, so eager to carry out this project that would benefit an entire region of Haiti, that we may have been a bit too enthusiastic and optimistic about the eventual results. However, out of the $21 million invested in the project, a very large portion, I would say at least 90 per cent, will help to improve the lives and well-being of the people of Haiti.
It was therefore unfair of the program's producers to criticize these activities the way they did, and to repeat the program a second time, which they did about two weeks ago after getting further information on CIDA activities in Haiti, as though they were trying to get the Canadian people up in arms about what CIDA is doing. Of course, they used this guy who probably helped the W5 producer to get his information, and I am referring to this Mr. Templeman, an official who had no responsibility himself for the project. I fail to understand, Mr. Speaker, why a responsible television network like CTV would have used an official who had certain views or opinions on the DRIP project but was not at all involved in the program, since he was assigned to the Canadian diplomatic service in Haiti.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about another aspect of the motion proposed by my colleague for Simcoe South, namely, fellowships. I mentioned earlier that my
colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon East had been awarded one of the fellowships, which are one of the major components of the IDRC's program. Since the motion mentions this component rather specifically, I shall say a few words on the subject.

The general objective of the fellowships program of IDRC is to improve the competence of professionals and researchers from developing countries, and to broaden the resource base of Canadian professionals concerned with international development. In the past year the program's orientation has shifted toward shorter term awards with particular emphasis on upgrading of professional, managerial, or research skills rather than long-term academic training.
The fellowships program offers several different categories of awards, and I will list a few of them. There are ten Pearson fellowships to be offered in the 1982-83 year with a total value of $375,000. In this program IDRC is offering carefully selected public servants a nine to twelve-month program in Canada to improve their professional and managerial skills. Each program involves a series of placements in government, industry, university, research centres and/or appropriate centres. For 1981-82, the field of concentration of agriculture. For 1982-83, awards will be made in the health field.
The purpose of the fellowship is to assist young public servants in developing countries to enhance themselves professionally so that they might better serve their country. They must be 25 to 35 years of age, have at least three years' working experience, and be citizens of developing countries. In order to be selected, candidates must be nominated by Canadian missions, undergo regional interviews and pass a final selection by an IRDC committee in Ottawa. The value of the award is the total of the actual cost of round-trip travel for the fellow and his or her family, research and Canadian travel up to $5,000, and a basic stipend of $16,000 with allowances for family, medical expenses, clothing and other necessities.
Pre and post-project awards are to provide training for individuals who have been or are to be associated with an IDRC supported project. The pre-project award will assist in the training of an individual who is key to a proposed IDRC project. The post-project award will upgrade the qualifications of an individual who has shown great promise during the life of the project. The training given should enable this individual to contribute to building up research capabilities in the home country. You now have, Mr. Speaker, a broader view of the program and how the beneficiaries of the bursaries are selected.

However, at the beginning of the second decade of the IDRC's existence, there is still much to be done, and I hope that the Canadian people and the members of this House will now have better understanding of the activities of the IDRC.
July 22, 1982

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity today to speak in this debate. Since some time has elapsed since we heard the motion, 1 am going to start out by reading the motion my colleague, the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart), has presented. It asks:
That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all communications, transcripts or notes of interviews, memos, notes of telephone conversations, applications for grants, bursaries and fellowships between the government through the International Development Research Centre and any other person or group requesting or being considered for financial grants from the International Development Research Centre, particularly relating to financial grants or fellowships or financial sponsorship to individuals who hold or held elected or appointed office in governments of other countries or who were or are members of recognized political parties in other foreign nations.
I have not heard any speakers so far give any logical reasons why the government should not supply this information. That is the bottom line of this whole debate. If such wonderful things are being done, as mentioned by the last speaker and by some others, why is the government hesitating to make this information public? That is all the motion asks. If it is such wonderful information and if the record is so wonderful, I would think the ministers would be falling all over each other to see who could present it first.
I believe hon. members on the government side will have an opportunity today to vote in favour of this motion and the government will then be required to present this information. If hon. members believe this has been such a wonderful program and that everything is hunky-dory and satisfactory, I would say to government members here that here is their wonderful chance to make it public and to vote in favour of this motion today. The government will then supply all this wonderful information it is talking about. That is all we ask.
We now have a freedom of information bill and we will see how it works pretty soon. But here is a chance to show that the government really believes in making information public. That is the bottom line to this whole debate, as I have just said.
In the report of the parliamentary task force on North-South relations it states that in 1978 the Treasury Board conducted a study on the effectiveness of food aid, but the results were never made public. Hon. members can find that on page 49 of the report.
Again, if the results were so wonderful and if this money is doing such marvellous things as feeding hungry people and enabling people to become self-sufficient, which is the object of the whole exercise, why was the report not made public? This sort of thing is what is bothering the people of Canada. It bothers me and it bothers my colleague, the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart). The request is reasonable. Just tell us what is going on and let us have the complete history. I think the chairman of the committee would be right up front if he said, "Let the people of Canada know what is going on".
International Development Research Centre
The information regarding interest rates charged to Third World countries is kept secret. That bothers me. I made a simple telephone call to the department some weeks ago to find out what the interest rate was on a large loan being made to one of the Third World countries. I was advised the information was not available, that it was secret. The information is even kept secret from members of Parliament. I do not think one should be trying to force something out of a civil servant, but he told me that this information is not even made available to Members of Parliament. I asked him if he made the information available to ministers. He hesitated. I do not know whether they do or not, but I imagine the minister of the department has access to it. If he is a minister worth his salt, he would know what is going on.
Here we are giving credit to countries at the expense of the people of Canada, yet the rate of interest charged is not made public. If it is a low interest rate and it can be justified, surely we can carry the judgment of the people of Canada to decide if the cause is worth while. Canadians are not illiterate. They would accept sound argument if sound argument was put forward. But to keep information secret and for us to be told that we cannot have it makes everyone suspicious.
In Canada banks are required to divulge the interest rates they charge. I do not know why the government does not make public the rates charged when we give lines of credit to other countries.
Canadians are compassionate people. We do not need to plead with the people of Canada to be compassionate when need arises. I think all political parties are compassionate. They want to help the needy. People may have different views on how to do that, but people are compassionate. Some may object to waste and extravagance. 1 do, and I am sure this party objects to waste and extravagance. I think any party in Canada should object to waste and extravagance.
We have certain objectives to meet. For instance, CIDA's written policy on food aid states that, "food aid from developed countries represents an attempt to bridge the gap between food production and food requirements in developing countries until self-sufficiency is achieved." "Until selfsufficiency is achieved" sounds like an excellent objective.
Let us look at some of the results and see what is going on. For instance, Cuba is in the communist bloc and yet we have been assisting that country.
When I was a boy I used to see people gathering iron, steel and metals around our coal mines. We would be paid two bits for bringing a load to the truck. We thought it was wonderful to get some money. That steel and other metals went to Japan. It was not very many years later that it came back to us in the form of bullets used against Canadian youth, men and women. I am a little leery about giving things to communist countries.
On May 20, 1980, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) explained in the House that Cuba was $10 million in arrears on a loan with terms of 3 per cent interest, seven years grace and 30 years maturity. At that time Cuba was two semi-annual payments in arrears. I have not been able to find

July 22, 1982
International Development Research Centre
out if Cuba has met the payments or whether they have been written off. But that information should be made available to the people of Canada. Why should we be lending money to Cuba at 3 per cent interest and 30 years maturity when we cannot help our home owners and our farmers who are going bankrupt and our businessmen who need money?
The government has a borrowing bill before us now for $7 billion. We will be paying interest probably in the range of 15 per cent to 21 per cent if we are lucky. The rate may be higher.
The New International Economic Order, for short, NIEO, is advocated by the United Nations. The object of this order is to transfer resources of countries that have worked hard to develop them and to transfer them to Third World countries. I find that somewhat bothersome.
The Brandt report worries me. I am advised that this report is strongly supported by our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). Whether or not that is true, I do not know, but it is certainly alleged that he supports it. The Brandt report says that to help develop nations we should increase foreign aid to 0.7 per cent of the gross national product. At the present time we are providing $1.23 billion per year in foreign aid. There are those who want it increased. I think we should be careful about this, especially when we see hungry people right in this country, when we see the living conditions of natives on reserves, when we see people losing their homes and their businesses, and when we see more than a million people unemployed who wonder where their next meal is coming from. We should remember that charity begins at home before we start increasing foreign aid.
The second recommendation is even more disturbing. The Brandt report recommended that a form of international income tax be levied on developed nations.
It recommended a form of international taxation or global taxation. It proposed that an international body have the authority to levy a tax on other countries for worth-while causes such as on arms trade, international investment, hydrocarbons and exhaustible minerals, luxury goods, military spending, the consumption of energy, international air travel, the use of the "international commons", ocean fishing, offshore oil and gas, seabed mining, the use of space orbits, radio communications, etc. Also it suggested a 0.5 per cent levy on all these things. If one takes a trip to China at one's own expense, he or she must pay a 0.5 per cent tax to this international body. Certainly that would be a wonderful way to raise money, but they do not mention how many international civil servants would be needed to do the job.
I would not support an international authority to levy taxes upon Canadians. Canada is a sovereign country. If we are to tax our people, our own governments will tax them, not some international body. I oppose this with all my might and strength because it is a ridiculous situation. If we ever get to the point where we provide taxing authority to the United Nations or to any other international body, the next step will be an international police force which will be able to pound
unwilling nations into submission. We should recognize that this is what would happen.
I was somewhat amazed when I read a statement of the former president of CIDA, Mr. Maurice Strong. I do not know him, but I have heard about him. He said that this idea was a prime objective, "as it provides the fairest and most dependable method of transferring resources".
We have plenty to do now right in our country with our resources. As a matter of fact, we are already helping other countries by bringing in oil, and our own oil wells are closed down.
I do not want to deal with that issue right now because I do not have the time, but the matter of interfering with national sovereignty should be watched very carefully. It may be done subtly and step by step, and eventually some world body will have control and authority to tax.
I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs, if he is supporting such a thing, will rise in the House and say so, or 1 would like to hear him rise and say that he will not support it. Also I would like to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say it, because there is a very subtle movement going on in the world today which is trying to get control of nations through the back door. If we ever get to the point where we are under the thumb of an international body, heaven help the people. Even this government is better than an international one. At least it has to report back to the people periodically.
There is something else with which I would like to deal in connection with the report. I should like to refer to a comparison which was conducted by an environmental board in the United States. It compared Iowa with Bangladesh. The member who spoke before me referred to Bangladesh. Both Iowa and Bangladesh cover the same area, in size. However, Iowa is rich in agriculture, while Bangladesh is desperately poor. The population of Iowa is two million and the population of Bangladesh is 78 million. We could simply transfer food from now to doomsday, but if we are to help the people of Bangladesh, we should help them to help themselves, to become self-sustaining and to start doing a little hard work along with receiving gifts from other countries. This is what undeveloped countries have to realize.
Let me give another example. Tanzania was once an exporter of foods. Scandinavian figures show that Tanzania's losses through self-inflicted agricultural decline are 250 per cent greater than the losses incurred because of higher oil prices. They are roughly equivalent to the foreign aid received between 1973 and 1980. Nyerere's policy of collectivizing farmland has ruined its agricultural system and has made beggars out of the people. This is not very helpful to the people of Tanzania. Would that be helping a country? This is only part of the dismal record.
From 1978 to 1981 Canada gave the government of Tanzania $91,541 million. The sum was broken down as follows: $78.92 million in the form of grants or straight gifts, $1,709 million for specific programs, and $10,912 million for food aid.
July 22, 1982

I would like to know what was done with that money. They are in worse shape now than in the years in which we gave them that money from 1978 to 1981.
What is happening? Are we building up a world slavery or something? Are we simply going to dish out money for a few big shots to use as they want while the masses go hungry? They have not fed the hungry of Bangladesh. We must remember that Canada forgave $71.9 million. We said that they did not have to pay it back at all; it was given to them. This was referred to on page 37 of the C1DA annual report of 1979-80. We should be giving aid to enable people of help themselves, not to make beggars of them. Equipment is fine, money is fine, but only if work is involved to make use of them so that they can become self-sustaining.
There are too many bleeding hearts in Canada who want to just give and give and give without expecting any results. We want the government to be accountable. This motion would be a step in the right direction. The government should be accountable for what it does. It should ensure that the money is being spent properly. Too much of our help is directed toward helping them continue with discredited communistic policies rather than helping the people. The losers are the rank and file people, the masses who obtain very little of the aid.
I wish the Government of Canada would realize that economic growth is achieved through hard work and incentive. Our farmers did not reach the level of production of today by depending upon government. It was hard work. It was the work of their brains, their backs, their arms and legs which produced the farms of the country. They produce and have produced tremendous amounts of food. There was incentive because they knew if they worked hard they could build up something for their wives, their children and the generations after them. This is what we must instil in the minds of people in these other countries. We want to help them to become selfsustaining. We do not want to become a welfare association for the world. We want an accounting of every cent which goes to these countries from the government.
Today we are contributing $1.23 billion. It should be doing a lot of good. I would like an accounting from government as to what it is doing when it takes $1.23 billion and sends it elsewhere at a time when many people in Canada are wondering where their next meal will come from. We are so hard up that the government starts capping the indexation of the pensions of retired public servants, many of whom are not even receiving enough money now to live properly. Their average wage is only $8,000 a year. Yet the government is capping indexing in that area. Certainly, if the average wage is $8,000, some wages are higher. If the government wanted to have a proper policy and had to take money from these people who spent their lives working for the government, why did they not start at the top instead of at the bottom? It should not have been done at all. Let us have an accounting of what the government is doing.

the International Development Research Centre had done, as have most of the members of the House, but I never realized how extensive and well respected the work of the centre was throughout the world. Basically it has a small budget compared to the other budgets we have, but it has been highly spoken of on almost every occasion that it has been referred to.
I refer the House to The Financial Post article by Philip Teasdale dated August 18, 1979. He says:
The agency, the brainchild of the late Lester Pearson, has a tiny (by foreign aid standards) annual budget of $38 million. But over the years it has earned a large reputation.
It was the first agency in the world to devote its efforts to giving scientific and technological advice-instead of just money-to the developing countries of the Third World.
Since June 10, and before, I have talked to officials at that particular centre. We should be very proud of what we have done, as Canadians, through this centre which is only a little over a decade old. It has involved 849 projects in 100 countries. It deals with life expectancy, adult literacy and, something that I found very significant, the research and development of traditional crops. We do not try to impose on those countries the production of crops that we have in Canada. We deal with crops they have such as millets and sorghum. We have had success in Bangladesh, Egypt, Panama, Zambia, the Philippines, Korea, Ghana, Tanzania and along the Amazon.
In forestry we are helping those regions of Africa where 50 per cent of the forests will be depleted by the year 2000, if assistance is not provided. We are also providing assistance in the area of health to Ecuador, Thailand and Sudan, particularly with regard to tropical diseases.
I believe that the people involved in this work on our behalf should not be spoken of in a partisan and derogatory way. We should be aware of what they are doing and be very proud of them.
If the hon. member has complaints about CIDA and certain of its functions, that is fine. As far as the International Development Research Centre is concerned, I have seen nothing I would not be proud of as a Canadian.
In June when this motion was first before us, I thought it would provoke a very profound debate, and that is why I was prepared. I was originally to be one of the initial speakers, but now I find myself winding up the debate.
On June 10, the hon. member for Simcoe South said that we had given $107,000 to the Belgian Congo for the development of nuts, but that the only nuts that had been developed were here on the Liberal benches. Well, you have to be a little crazy to be a politician anyway, whether you are a member of the opposition, the NDP or the Liberal Party. That is acceptable. Then the hon. member went too far. He called us a cell of leftleaning demagogues headed by the right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). To be called a nut is one thing, but to be called a left-leaning demagogue is not acceptable to anyone on this side of the House.
I will conclude on a certain note of facetiousness, because I do not believe that the hon. member is really complaining
about the work that the centre is doing. I think he is complaining about waste in certain agencies, and I think that kind of complaint should be guarded to a certain extent. When an agency can say that the opposition has looked at its work and has indicated it is doing a good job, it is like getting a passing grade. I believe this is acceptable because it is the role of democracy.
I would like to end by saying that the International Development Research Centre is one of the bright lights of Canadian government, of whatever political stripe, and should be encouraged and fostered. As Canadians we should be carrying on these duties abroad because this is what we do well.

Mr. Speaker, we are not talking about aid in this debate. All hon. members and all Canadians want to give aid where it is needed. We are talking about freedom of information and the fact that this government witholds that information no matter what subject it is on. We are also talking about the fact that the government is wasteful and a poor manager.
We want to consider the basic reason why I brought this matter up and put it on the Order Paper. My colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), asked a question, as reported in Hansard on December 16, 1980, as to why Mr. Manley was going to be given $60,000 to come to Canada to study under an IDRC grant. That is what we want to know. Why is the government so left-leaning? Every report that I read which concerns international development is left-leaning.
On November 13, 1980, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) why this country gave $100 million to Jamaica, $10 million as a grant, when Mr. Manley was prime minister. But when Mr. Seaga was in power from 1980 to 1981, all the government gave him was $2.3 million. A left-winger like Mr. Manley can get $100 million but Mr. Seaga can only get $2.3 million. I think it is pretty self-evident as to which way the government leans. I have all the meaningful figures on Jamaica here.
What does the government have to hide? The IDRC is a sacred cow, just like CIDA. What does the government have to hide? There is a bill presently before the House which proposes deindexing, but foreign aid is indexed. It is indexed to GNP. It is indexed from 0.05 per cent now, in 1982-83, rising to 0.075 per cent by 1990. The budget of CIDA is up $188.8 million. Where is the fairness and restraint there? Where is the freedom of information? Show us what the IDRC is doing and show us which countries the aid is going to.

1 believe many areas in the country could be almost selfsufficient in all respects. There are others, of course, that could not, and there are others which should not be localized. I can understand the role of the federal government in ensuring that

there is equity across Canada for as long as we are all Canadians. I hope that we all continue to be Canadians, as we know Canadians today, for many years into the future. I can understand the federal government's wanting to have control over vast areas of the economy so as to provide equity, such as by way of the established programs financing, or to provide health services and post-secondary education which is of the same standard all across Canada or at least provide these services so that there are no areas which cannot develop and have the same health care services and education as other areas of the country, no matter whether in the maritimes, in Newfoundland, British Columbia or in Saskatchewan. I can think of some areas where we should localize and try to become selfsufficient, such as the Town of Meadow Lake within my own constituency. We have a large sawmill there which is feeling the pinch because of bad economic times. But the waste material from that sawmill is burned off in what is called a beehive and all the energy goes up into the air in smoke. It is very possible, and the technology is there for that sawmill to provide the electricity, that it could be changed from thermal to electrical to provide the entire electrical needs for the Town of Meadow Lake and provide a surplus for use in other regions. Where something like this can be done, they should supply their own needs in terms of energy, and the excess pumped into a central grid system. The province should be the collector of the surplus and distribute it to regions that are not self-sufficient in terms of energy, namely electrical requirements, the other towns and cities throughout the province.
The same should be done on a national scale. Surpluses should be distributed to other regions of the country. In those areas where there is a surplus of market vegetables, grain or energy, after supplying the needs in Canada, the rest should be exported to the international market.
Something else comes to mind, the amount of vegetables imported into this country. At peak times we import about 80 per cent of our vegetables. This may seem like a small matter, but we have the ability to produce those here. If we did that, we would not have to rely on other countries to the extent we do at present.
Canada could become the most self-sufficient country in the world. We have a little over 24 million people. There are thousands of miles from Bonavista to Vancouver Island from the 49th parallel up to the 60th and beyond. People are spread over that area. There are some problems in transporting the commodities to all these people, but it can be done.
In Canada there is a wealth of resources. Even if we only used oil for our energy needs, we could be self-sufficient. However, in some areas alternate energies can be developed. Canada should be self-sufficient in energy by the goal year of 1990. We should have been self-sufficient long before that. However, under the National Energy Program, which has been a flop, the goal is 1990. I do not believe the government will achieve that goal and that we will have energy self-sufficiency

July 22, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
or security of energy supplies by then, even though we certainly should have.
This is a very hard time in many parts of our manufacturing sector, mainly central Canada, Ontario and Quebec. There are a great many problems in the shoe and textile industry. That should not be the case. That presents a real problem for the government. When a pair of shoes imported from Brazil or Italy can be purchased for $50 to $70 and a comparable shoe of Canadian manufacture sells for $125, it is hard to convince the consumer to buy the Canadian product. I can appreciate that the government has difficult problems to come to grips with. There is the fine balance of whether to manufacture the product here and place tariffs on imports, which does not give the consumer a break, or whether to cause more unemployment. I am sure there are many arguments in the Liberal caucus on that problem.
Before my time runs out, I would like to talk about some expenditures that could be cut by the federal government which to this point have not served a useful purpose. I know that when they were started, the intentions were good and honourable. The first cut I would suggest would be to abolish the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. That department has held back our aboriginal people, the treaty Indians, for many years. It has not substantially improved the living conditions on Indian reserves. In fact, they have likely deteriorated since Confederation.
In the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development the ratio of government employees to treaty Indians is 33 to one. Some classroom teacher-student ratios are not that good. Some may think the Indian people should be treated like children, and in some cases they have been, but that should stop. There is a flagrant waste of money within that department. I do not lay the entire blame on the federal government, but it is their responsibility.
The department does have to protect some rights, as well as treaties and agreements that have been signed in the past. I suggest the alternative to a large overwhelming Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development would be an Indian rights protection office. It could be much smaller. More control could be turned over to the Indian people so that everything that happens in their everyday lives would not be dictated by a department of government.
There are many public employees within the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development with good vision for Indian people. They are not at fault. This is part of a system out of control. Those people could find many useful places in society without the frustration of having to work for the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I do not totally condemn advertising. However, this is an area where a cut could be made. It could substantially reduce our national debt and our ever-increasing yearly deficits. Government advertising and polling done by the government could be cut to at least half. Hundreds of millions of dollars are spent by this government on advertising, which quite often is of a partisan nature. If it were only done to educate the
people of Canada, that would be fine. However, quite often it loses that significance and there is more partisanship than information.
There is something else that can be done to turn this country around. I will be making representations to the Committee on Parliamentary Reform which will be sitting this summer. First, the upper house should be changed from a patronage Senate where members are appointed in a partisan manner to a council of provinces with two or three democratically-elected people from each province. These people would run for reelection in the provincial elections.
This would give some increased control over what happens within government without costing a great deal. In fact, it would likely cost less than the present patronage Senate system. It would overcome the complaints of many Canadians about having representation by population. That has been a destructive force in this country and needs to be changed.
An elected council of the provinces to replace the Senate would give regional representation. It would be a meaningful upper house which could scrutinize the work done in this House. That is a proposal I will be making to the Parliamentary Committee on Regulatory Reform.
I see my time is rapidly running out. I think Members of Parliament need to have more influence and more input into what happens in government. Too often things happen without consultation with Members of Parliament and their constituents. There should be that consultation because we have a large and vast country. My constituency is some 2,000 miles from Ottawa. Many other constituencies in Canada are 3,000 miles, and perhaps more, away from Ottawa. I do not condemn the government for this, but members of the cabinet cannot appreciate all the problems across this very vast land. Many government programs are band-aid programs. I do not always agree with programs of that kind, but if the government is going to use band-aid measures to patch up some of the holes in our economy and to solve other very pressing problems, there should be consultation with local governments, provincial governments and especially Members of Parliament who are democratically elected by their constituents.
Just before I close 1 would like to pay tribute to my wife Mona and our three children, Bree, Ashala and Nikki. I was talking with them tonight, and they think it is insane that some Members of Parliament have sat here over the summer and not really contributed very much. My children will be going back to school very soon, and I am very anxious to get home and to spend some of the summer with them before they go back to school. I want also to hear what the problems in my constituency are.

I will make a brief reference to a well-known economist, Ken Galbraith who, in his book "The New Industrial State", wrote the following:
Like private consumption, any new public service quickly becomes a part of the accustomed standard of living. Once given, support to schools or hospitals or public transportation cannot be readily withdrawn.
It strikes me that that is the situation we face today. This government has provided social programs, economic development programs and defence programs-you name it-and the Canadian people have come to expect the government to deliver these programs. In other words, they have become a part of our accustomed standards and way of life, just as Galbraith told us. If we are to continue giving support to these expectations, then Bill C-125 must be passed.
The combined opposition can keep on talking about briefcases and cook books, but if they deny passage of this bill, they will in essence be saying no to some $7 billion for our old age pensioners; some $2.5 billion for those who receive the guaranteed income supplement; some $250 million for spouses allowance payments; some $2.3 billion for family allowance payments; some $110 million for medical research grants; some $23 million for Indian and northern health services, the ones just deprecated by the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish); some $24 million for the administration of our airports across the country; and some $500 million to run VIA Rail. The opposition will be saying no to some $29 million to run the CNR and CN Marine; some $672 million for the war veterans allowance and civilian war allowance benefits; some $600 million for the payment of war veterans pensions; and some $470 million to run our transport system.
The passage of this bill would allow $1.7 million to be used to protect consumers across the country; some $7 million to promote economic development in certain regions; some $2.3 billion for unemployment insurance benefits; some $96 million for fishermen's benefits; some $200 million for direct job creation; some $200 million for employment training; some $4.6 million toward easing the adjustment of immigrants in our country; some $236 million for the efficient use of our energy resources; some $135 million to run Petro-Canada so that we can increase Canada's energy supply; some $540 million to run our security systems, our prisons, the RCMP and the like; some $70 million to keep our federal courts open and running; some $20 million for Canertech, which is the imaginative scheme put forward for renewable energy resources; some $575 million to provide research grants for science and technology; and some $4.5 million to promote and ensure a safe and healthy work place.
This list could go on and on. These are the programs which are fully supported by Canadians, and we do not intend to see them denied. We cannot say no to small business when it comes to the $400 million allocation announced on June 28 in the budget. We cannot say no to home buyers. They need the $300 million to purchase their first homes. We cannot say no to the construction industry, which requires incentives so that it can start building again. We cannot say no to those who seek

non-profit and co-operative housing, some 27,500 units, and we cannot say no to those who wish to take advantage of home renovation plans and programs which amount to some $30 million across the country and benefit urban areas where unemployment is the highest.
Our financial needs-our deficit, if hon. members want to call it that-depend on how much money we can collect through taxes and how much we spend on our social programs and policies to run our country. If the economy were strong, we would not have to borrow this money. That fact is clear. However, revenues have decreased; hence, the high deficit. In fact, it has been calculated that $4 of every $5 increase in the deficit is due to lack of funds coming in.
The situation we are facing in Canada is also faced by many other industrialized countries. That situation has caused what is commonly called a world recession here, in the U.S., in West Germany, in Italy, in France and in the U.K. The deficit, therefore, is not because we are spending more money on new things; it is because we want to honour the commitments we have made in the past, and those commitments now cost more.
This is very much unlike what is happening south of the border, where the Reagan administration has chosen to cut social costs. I am sure my hon. friend across the aisle would be prepared to do that, as Tories usually are in difficult times.

Mr. Speaker, let us look at this deficit from the perspective of 1968, when this government first came to power. After a depression, two world wars and the building of a country, the total national debt in Canada stood at $17 billion. That was the total national debt. Now, 14 years later the national debt is $145 billion. In fact, the deficit this year is higher than the total accumulated debt after the first 100 years. Surely Canadians can ask whether government has better control in terms of its expenditures.
Members of the House know that the Auditor General, the chief witness before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, has said that spending control has simply gone; it is not there, that government spending is out of control. The government can say whatever it wants, but the verdict of independent people with expertise who looked at the accounts, is that government spending is out of control.
The Minister of Labour said that the deficit was not going to cause Canadian business any great difficulty because business was not competing for moneys. He justified that by saying that business was not in the money market now because it was in a down turn. That is true. But surely the question must be asked why. The answer is that it is because of the three budgets brought in by the Minister of Finance. First, the National Energy Program took away an industry's resources and its ability to give us energy self-sufficiency. The second budget of the Minister of Finance was condemmed universally across the country. People were absolutely shocked to learn in the third budget that the deficit was $20 billion and growing.
What this government has not been able to instil in Canadians is confidence. It has been unable to instil investor confidence. When the Minister of Labour said that there is no problem, that the government is not going to be able to raise interest rates because only the government will be in the money markets, that is true. But I say to the minister that is hardly a reason or a solution to the economic problems of the day.
This government uses one stock answer when anyone criticizes the deficit. Government members ask, "What will you cut out?" The extrapolation of that argument is this, that any deficit, any spending, any hardship on Canadian taxpayers is justified. If you have a problem, you have one solution. You throw more money at it. The Minister of Labour today literally took us on a cook's tour of the Blue Book of the expenditures of the government. He was saying "Look, we are doing all these wonderful things for Canadians, and therefore, we should continue". But he never answered the question that because of government policies-to a great degree because of government policies-1.3 million Canadians are unemployed. He never addressed the question which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) mentioned in Toronto yesterday, that is that we could be losing a whole generation of young Canadians because they cannot get into the labour market. 1 hope the National Training Act works. But I want to tell the minister and members opposite that you can have a training act and an apprenticeship program, but when a company has to cut back employees, who are the first ones to go? In most cases the first ones to go are the ones without experience or those who do not have their journeyman's papers. That is the situation we now face in Canada. A very tough decision will have to be made. No one in public life wants to make that decision. There must be a parliamentary committee with the power to cut expenditures before the fact rather than having the Public Accounts Committee look at expenditures after the fact. The Public Accounts Committee looks at the accounts roughly two years after the expenditures have taken place. But that money has already gone. It is already spent. What we need is a close examination of expenditures before they are made.
The government uses two arguments, first, that it would not be in trouble if only it were getting more revenue, and second, that if the revenue were not dropping, the government would not be in any difficulty. It reminds me of the person who says that he really has no problem balancing his or her own personal books. The only problem is that there is always too much month left at the end of the money. That is literally where this government is at. But when Canadians have difficulty and when they do not have enough money for their expenditures, what choice do they have? What do they do? They can go to the local banker and ask to float a loan. But for how long and how often can they do that? Eventually, what people have to do is to bring expenditures in line with revenue. That is the only avenue they have. They cannot say that they are going to continue spending more money because they know that if they
